lessons.title: Describe Data by Range and Interquartile Range
lessons.objective: I can find the range and the interquartile range of a data set and use them to describe how spread out the data is.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain what the spread of a data set is using the words range, quartile, interquartile range, and vary.

concept.heading: How spread out is the data?
concept.intro: A measure of center like the median tells you where the data sits. It does not tell you how far apart the values are. Two classes can share the same median and still look nothing alike. Range and interquartile range are the two numbers that describe that spread.
concept.keyIdea: Measures of Variability: Range & IQR. Formula: Range = Maximum − Minimum | IQR = Q3 − Q1. 1. Range measures the total spread across the entire data set. 2. IQR (Interquartile Range) measures the spread of the middle 50% of data. 3. Both are non-negative distance measures of variability

worked.title: Watch me measure the spread of the test scores
lines: Here are 20 history test scores in order: 68, 70, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 80, 82, 83, 84, 85, 86, 86, 88, 88, 90, 90, 93, 94. Ordering them first is what makes every step after this possible.
Range: I subtract the least value from the greatest. 94 − 68 = 26. The scores span 26 points from end to end.
Now the quartiles. The median splits the 20 scores into two halves of 10. The median is halfway between the 10th and 11th values: (83 + 84) ÷ 2 = 83.5.
Q1 is the median of the lower 10 values: halfway between 75 and 76, so Q1 = 75.5. Q3 is the median of the upper 10: halfway between 88 and 88, so Q3 = 88.
Interquartile range: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 88 − 75.5 = 12.5. The middle half of the students' scores differed by only 12.5 points, even though the full range was 26.
linesEs: Aquí están 20 calificaciones del examen de historia en orden: 68, 70, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 80, 82, 83, 84, 85, 86, 86, 88, 88, 90, 90, 93, 94. Ordenarlas primero es lo que hace posible cada paso siguiente.
Rango: resto el valor menor del mayor. 94 − 68 = 26. Las calificaciones abarcan 26 puntos de extremo a extremo.
Ahora los cuartiles. La mediana divide las 20 calificaciones en dos mitades de 10. La mediana está a la mitad entre el 10.º y el 11.º valor: (83 + 84) ÷ 2 = 83.5.
Q1 es la mediana de los 10 valores inferiores: a la mitad entre 75 y 76, así que Q1 = 75.5. Q3 es la mediana de los 10 superiores: a la mitad entre 88 y 88, así que Q3 = 88.
Rango intercuartílico: Q3 − Q1 = 88 − 75.5 = 12.5. La mitad central de las calificaciones de los estudiantes se diferenció en solo 12.5 puntos, aunque el rango completo fue de 26.
worked.titleEs: Mírame medir la dispersión de las calificaciones del examen

together.title: Let's do one together
lines: Class A's box plot reads: least 62, Q1 74, median 81, Q3 87, greatest 90. Find the range first.
Range = 90 − 62 = 28 points from the lowest score to the highest.
Now the IQR: subtract Q1 from Q3. IQR = 87 − 74 = 13 points across the middle half.
Say what each one means: the whole class's scores span 28 points, but the middle half of the class is packed into 13 points.
linesEs: El diagrama de caja de la clase A indica: mínimo 62, Q1 74, mediana 81, Q3 87, máximo 90. Halla primero el rango.
Rango = 90 − 62 = 28 puntos desde la calificación más baja hasta la más alta.
Ahora el rango intercuartílico: resta Q1 de Q3. Q3 − Q1 = 87 − 74 = 13 puntos en la mitad central.
Di lo que significa cada uno: las calificaciones de toda la clase abarcan 28 puntos, pero la mitad central de la clase se concentra en 13 puntos.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers that describe spread: the range covers all the data, and the interquartile range covers only the middle half.
vocabulary.example: Range 26 covers 68 to 94; IQR 12.5 covers only 75.5 to 88

vocabulary.definition: The distance from the least value to the greatest value, found by subtracting: greatest − least.
One of the three values that cut an ordered data set into four equal-sized groups.
The distance across the middle half of the data, found by subtracting the first quartile from the third: Q3 − Q1.
vocabulary.example: 88 − 75.5 = 12.5 — the width of the box on a box plot

vocabulary.definition: How much the values in a data set differ from one another — whether they sit close together or far apart.
vocabulary.example: Close together = low variability; spread apart = high variability

vocabulary.definition: A single number that describes the spread of a whole data set. The range and the IQR are both measures of variation.
vocabulary.example: One number stands in for the spread of all 20 scores

vocabulary.definition: The least or greatest value in a data set, far from the rest.
vocabulary.example: An extreme value stretches the range.

title: The Consistency Cup
mission: Compare how spread out a team’s results are. Decide whether the range or the middle half tells the more useful story.
investigate: Predict the range and interquartile range of the starting results.
Keep the median fixed while increasing the range. What did you change?
Make the middle half more tightly grouped without changing the minimum or maximum.
create: Build two sets of eight results with the same range but different interquartile ranges. Explain which team is more consistent in its middle half.

support.prompt: A data set runs from a least value of 12 to a greatest value of 30. What is the range?
feedback: 12 is the least value, not the distance between the two ends.
21 is halfway between 12 and 30 — that is a center, not a spread.
30 is the greatest value, not the distance between the two ends.
hints: Range asks how far it is from one end of the data to the other.
Find the greatest value and the least value, then subtract.

support.prompt: On a box plot, Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 36. What is the interquartile range?
feedback: 28 is halfway between 20 and 36 — that is a middle, not a width.
36 is Q3 by itself, not the distance from Q1 to Q3.
That is 36 + 20. The IQR is a difference, so subtract.
hints: The IQR is the width of the box on a box plot.
The box runs from Q1 to Q3, so subtract Q1 from Q3.

support.prompt: Which measure of spread uses ONLY the middle half of the data?
support.explanation: The IQR runs from Q1 to Q3, which is exactly the middle half of the values. The range is the distance from the minimum to the maximum; interior values do not enter that subtraction.
feedback: The range stretches from the least value to the greatest; it is calculated from those two extremes.
The median is a measure of center, not of spread.
The mode is the most common value — also not a measure of spread.
hints: One is measured across the box on a box plot; the other whisker to whisker.
The box holds the middle 50% of the data.
Q1 to Q3 is the middle half.

support.prompt: Two classes both have a median score of 81. Class A's IQR is 13 and Class B's IQR is 8. Which statement is true?
choices: Class B has a higher median
The middle half of Class B's scores is less spread out
Class B's highest score is greater
support.explanation: A smaller IQR means the middle half of the data is packed into a shorter stretch, so Class B's middle half varies less. The medians are equal, so nothing there separates them.
feedback: Both medians are 81 — they are the same.
The IQR says nothing about how many students are in a class.
The IQR describes only the middle half; it says nothing about the highest score.
hints: A smaller IQR means a narrower box.
A narrower box means the middle half of the values sit closer together.
Which class has the smaller IQR?

steps: Step 3: The middle half of the data spans 100 units.
support.explanation: Step 2 should subtract, not add: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 58 − 42 = 16. Step 3 then reads: the middle half of the data spans 16 units — which must be smaller than the range of 20, because the middle half is part of the whole span.
hints: Compare the IQR in Step 2 to the range in Step 1.
Can the middle half of the data be wider than all of the data?
IQR = Q3 − Q1, a subtraction.

core.prompt: A box plot shows: least 68, Q1 75.5, median 83.5, Q3 88, greatest 94. What are the range and the IQR?
core.explanation: Range = 94 − 68 = 26. IQR = 88 − 75.5 = 12.5. The range covers the whole span; the IQR covers only the box.
feedback: These are swapped: the range must be at least as large as the IQR.
83.5 is the median, a measure of center, not the width of the box.
hints: Do the whiskers first: greatest − least.
Then the box: Q3 − Q1.

core.prompt: Team A's salaries have a range of $14M and an IQR of $7M. Team B's have a range of $7M and an IQR of $2.5M. Both teams have the same median salary. What does this tell a player?
choices: Team B's salaries cluster much more tightly around the median
Team B's highest salary is greater
core.explanation: Both measures of variation are smaller for Team B, so its salaries vary less: a typical player is more likely to earn close to the median. Team A spreads much wider in both directions.
feedback: The medians are equal, so neither team pays more at the middle.
Neither measure of variation says anything about how many players there are.
Team A's greatest salary is $15M, which is larger than Team B's $9M.
hints: Compare the two ranges, then compare the two IQRs.
Smaller numbers mean the values sit closer together.
Both of Team B's numbers are smaller.

steps: Step 2: The range of 45 shows that a typical value differs from the others by about 45.
Step 3: So this data set has high variability everywhere.
core.explanation: Step 2 overreads the range. The range only reports the distance between the two extremes — here it is large because of the single value 60. Five of the six values sit between 15 and 25, a span of just 10. The IQR (about 7) shows that the middle of the data barely varies at all.
hints: Look at where the six values actually sit.
How far apart are the five values other than 60?
Which measure of variation ignores the extremes?

steps: Setup: Class A: least 62, Q1 74, median 81, Q3 87, greatest 90.
Setup: Class B: least 70, Q1 76, median 81, Q3 84, greatest 90.
Step 1: Both classes have a median of 81.
Step 2: Both classes reached the same greatest score, 90.
Step 3: So the two classes performed the same overall.
stretch.explanation: Step 3 ignores variability. Class A's range is 28 and its IQR is 13; Class B's range is 20 and its IQR is 8. Class B's scores are far less spread out, so 75% of Class B scored 76 or more, while a quarter of Class A scored below 74. Equal medians and equal maximums do not make two distributions the same.
hints: What have you NOT compared yet?
Compute both ranges and both IQRs.
Which class has the narrower box?

stretch.prompt: Two students both scored 80 on a make-up test — one joins Class A (range 28, IQR 13) and one joins Class B (range 20, IQR 8). Both classes have a median of 81. Predict how each class's IQR changes, and explain your reasoning.
stretch.explanation: Each new score of 80 lands just below the median of 81, which is inside the box for both classes. Adding a value inside the middle of the data pulls the quartiles slightly toward the center, so each IQR either stays the same or shrinks a little; neither can grow much, because nothing was added out at the extremes. The ranges do not change at all, since 80 is neither a new least nor a new greatest value for either class. The comparison holds: Class B's scores stay the more tightly clustered of the two.
hints: Where does 80 fall relative to each class's box?
A value added inside the box cannot stretch the box outward.
Does 80 change either class's least or greatest value?
